title: Property testing and reproducible numerical evidence
outcome: Combine hand-derived cases, generated inputs and invariants so that a plausible but incorrect transformation cannot pass by comparing only to itself.
key_terms: The `Test` package providing `@test`, `@test_throws` and `@testset` for recording checks and their results.
A check that a rule holds across many generated inputs rather than for one hand-picked example.
A test that compares outputs for related inputs, such as confirming that permuting inputs permutes outputs the same way.
A fixed starting value for a random generator, so generated test inputs and any failing case can be reproduced.
A property every valid output must satisfy, such as normalized weights being nonnegative and summing to one.
approach: `probabilities` rejects empty, nonfinite, negative and all-zero weights, divides by the largest weight to avoid overflow and then normalizes. Tests combine three kinds of evidence: hand-derived asymmetric cases, properties checked on generated inputs from `Xoshiro(140)`, and invariants such as unchanged input and ratio preservation.

exercises.title: Derive an oracle
exercises.task: Compute probabilities for weights `[2, 5, 3]` by hand.
exercises.answer: The hand-derived asymmetric case prevents a uniform-output bug from passing.
exercises.why: The weights `[2, 5, 3]` total 10, so the probabilities are 2/10, 5/10 and 3/10.
exercises.wrong: Checking only `[1, 1, 1]` lets a function that always returns equal shares pass, because the correct answer is uniform too.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `probabilities(values) ≈ [0.2, 0.5, 0.3]` and that the ratio of the second to the first is 2.5.

exercises.title: Diagnose overflow
exercises.hint: The desired probabilities are still well-defined.
exercises.answer: Scaling by the maximum gives `[1, 1]`, then divides by 2 without overflowing.
exercises.why: `1e308 + 1e308` exceeds `floatmax(Float64)` and becomes `Inf`, while dividing by the maximum first gives `[1, 1]` and then `[0.5, 0.5]`.
exercises.wrong: Dividing each weight by `sum(weights)` directly returns `[0, 0]` here because every weight is divided by infinity.

exercises.title: Test a permutation
exercises.task: Swap the first and last weights and predict the output.
exercises.expected: The first and last probabilities swap.
exercises.answer: Equivariance checks alignment and catches accidental sorting.
exercises.why: Swapping the first and last weights to `[3, 5, 2]` should give `[0.3, 0.5, 0.2]`, because each output is tied to its own input position.
exercises.wrong: An implementation that sorts weights first returns the same order for both inputs and passes sum-to-one checks.
exercises.verify: Example B checks `probabilities(values[permutation]) ≈ result[permutation]` on 20 generated inputs.

exercises.title: Find a weak property
exercises.task: Explain why sum-to-one alone cannot verify weighting.
exercises.answer: Properties constrain behavior from different directions; one broad invariant is insufficient.
exercises.why: A uniform output always sums to 1, so the sum property cannot tell correct weighting from ignoring the weights.
exercises.wrong: Relying on `sum(result) ≈ 1` as the only test gives confidence that is not earned.
exercises.verify: Combine the sum property with the hand case and the scaling property `probabilities(7 .* values) ≈ result`.

exercises.title: Add an input contract
exercises.task: Specify how negative, all-zero and nonfinite inputs should behave.
exercises.hint: Do not invent a replacement distribution.
exercises.answer: A rejected input gives the caller a chance to correct the model rather than silently changing its meaning.
exercises.why: Negative weights, all zeros and NaN or Inf each violate the definition, so `ArgumentError` lets the caller fix the model.
exercises.wrong: Clamping negatives to zero or returning a uniform vector for all zeros changes the model's meaning without telling the caller.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `ArgumentError` for empty, `[Inf, 1]` and `[NaN]`; example A covers `[0, 0]` and `[1, -1]`.

exercises.title: Transfer to a regression library
exercises.task: Propose properties for predictions from a fitted exact line.
exercises.expected: Known points, shape preservation and permutation alignment.
exercises.answer: Tests should detect coefficient swaps, row reordering and missing intercepts independently of the fitting implementation.
exercises.why: For a line with known intercept 1 and slope 2, predictions at x = 0 and 1 must be 1 and 3, the output length must match the input, and reordering rows must reorder predictions.
exercises.wrong: Deriving expected predictions from the fitted coefficients of the same code cannot catch swapped coefficients.
exercises.verify: Write these properties with literal coefficients, as in `predict([1, 2], [0, 1]) == [1, 3]` from lesson julia-021.

checks_note: `probabilities([3]) == [1]` covers the single-weight case. The final three lines combine a hand-derived answer, a check that `values` still equals `before`, and the ratio 2.5, which holds because normalizing divides both entries by the same total.
